The residue of $14$ modulo $6$ is the integer $0 \leq r < 6$ such that

\[ 14 \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6). \]

Method 1

To find the residue $r,$ we need to write $14$ as an integer multiple of $6,$ plus the residue $r.$

We note that $14 \equiv 2\,(\textrm{mod}\,6)$ because

\[ 14 = 2 \cdot 6 + {\color{blue}{2}} . \]

Therefore, the residue of $14$ modulo $6$ is ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

Method 2

We can use the subtraction property:

\begin{align*} 14 &\equiv 14 - 0 &&(\textrm{mod}\,6) \\[3pt] &\equiv 14 - 2 \cdot 6 &&(\textrm{mod}\,6) \\[3pt] &\equiv 14 - 12 &&(\textrm{mod}\,6)\\[3pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{2}} &&(\textrm{mod}\,6) \end{align*}

Therefore, the residue of $14$ modulo $6$ is ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Determining the Last Few Digits of a Number

question.text: Let $a$ be a positive integer. Construct an expression that gives a two-digit number consisting of the last two digits of $150a+130.$
question.explanation:
Let $b=150a+130.$ Note that $b$ is positive. Now, let $d_4,$ $d_3,$ $d_2,$ and $d_1$ be the last four digits of the number $a{:}$

\[ a = \ldots d_4d_3 d_2 d_1 \]

Then, $a$ can be written in expanded form as

\begin{align*} a &= \cdots + 1000d_4 + 100d_3 + 10d_2 + d_1 \\[5pt] &= 100(\cdots + 10d_4 + d_3) + 10d_2 + d_1. \end{align*}

Now, we compute the residue of $a$ modulo $100{:}$

\begin{align*} a &\equiv 100(\cdots + 10d_4 + d_3) + 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0\cdot (\cdots + 10d_4 + d_3) + 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0 + 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \\[5pt] &\equiv 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \end{align*}

Notice that $10d_2 + d_1$ is the two-digit number consisting of the last two digits of $a.$

Finally, since $b =150a+130,$ and \[ 150\equiv 50, \qquad 130\equiv 30 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,100) \] we have the following: \begin{align*} b&\equiv10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \\[5pt] 150a+130&\equiv 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \\[5pt] 50a+30&\equiv 10d_2 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,100) \end{align*}

Therefore, the expression that gives the last digit of $150a+130$ is the following:

\[ \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}50a+30} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{mod}}\: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}100} \]

question.text: Let $a$ be a positive integer. Construct an expression that gives the last digit of $21a+14.$
question.explanation:
Let $b=20a+14.$ Note that $b$ is positive. Now, let $d_3,$ $d_2,$ and $d_1$ be the last three digits of the number $b{:}$

\[ b = \ldots d_3 d_2 d_1 \]

Then, $b$ can be written in expanded form as follows:

\begin{align*} b &= \cdots + 100d_3 + 10d_2 + d_1 \\[5pt] &= 10(\cdots + 10d_3 + d_2) + d_1 \end{align*}

Now, we compute the residue of $b$ modulo $10{:}$

\begin{align*} b &\equiv 10(\cdots + 10d_3 + d_2) + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0\cdot (\cdots + 10d_3 + d_2) + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0 + d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \\[5pt] &\equiv d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \end{align*}

Notice that $d_1$ is the last digit of $b.$

Finally, since $b = 21a + 14,$ and \[ 21\equiv 1, \qquad 14\equiv 4 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,10) \] we have the following: \begin{align*} b&\equiv d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \\[5pt] 21a+14&\equiv d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \\[5pt] 1\cdot a+4&\equiv d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10)\\[5pt] a+4&\equiv d_1 &&(\textrm{mod}\,10) \end{align*}

Therefore, the expression that gives the last digit of $21a+14$ is the following:

\[ \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a+4} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{mod}}\: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}10} \]
